caption: The hangar mouth frames it better than any terminal gate — the plane, held still in a dark rectangle of concrete.
Tensile canopies in a row, a person at the peak. The structure is the silhouette.
A child sits where the arch meets the light. Everything else is shadow and LED.
The alley compresses everything — balconies, pipes, daylight — into one narrow slice of city.
A building facade at dusk: grid against sky, palm trees holding the edge.
An old bungalow holding its ground. Hanging plants, orange shutters, a modern block rising quietly behind.
The harbour on a grey day — ferries packed together like they are in no hurry at all.
A carved teak door from another century, still answering to the street.
Indo-Saracenic in monochrome — the ornament reads louder without colour.
The curved stair bisects a wall of hard light. Plants below, washing above.
A lane compressed to a slit of blue sky — a figure, an auto, a flag making it lived-in.
Fatma Villa, 1936. The ochre wall keeps its date on a small plaque while the street moves past.
Tiled roofs, latticed walls, one modern tower in the distance: the city in three layers.
The temple gate in deep red under a blue sky — ornament as elevation.
Tensile canopy from below at the Earthquake Museum — geometry that remembers by sheltering.
Cable-stayed geometry at dusk, a crescent moon caught in the pylon cables.
